Formula.Formula:
'

Heat Exchanger Overview

This model represents a thermodynamic heat balance on a simple counter current heat exchanger.

The input expressions are:

  • side1In - a flash result or similar representing the inlet fluid on side 1.
  • side1Dp - pressure drop across side 1, (inlet pressure - outlet pressure).
  • side2In - a flash result or similar representing the inlet fluid on side 2.
  • side1Dp - pressure drop across side 2, (inlet pressure - outlet pressure).
  • T2Out - outlet temperature of side 2. Can be empty.
  • dt - temperature difference between side 1 inlet and side 2 outlet. This is only used if T2Out is empty.

The outlet expressions are:

  • duty - the energy flow from side 2 to side 1.
  • lmtd - the log mean temperature difference.
  • side1Out - the flash result for the side 1 outlet fluid.
  • side2Out - the flash result for the side 2 outlet fluid.

It is assumed that both inlet fluids are completely known. This of course means the flow and compositions of the outlets are also known and because the pressure drops are also inputs, the outlet pressures are known.

The temperature of the side 2 outlet is either directly supplied by input expression T2Out or can be calculated from the side 1 inlet temperature and the supplied temperature approach from inlet expression dt.

This allows the conditions of the side 2 outlet to be evaluated, leaving only the side 1 outlet unknown. However it only needs one additional intensive variable and that can be supplied by doing an energy balance around the exchanger to give the side 1 outlet enthalpy. This calculation is perform right in the formula for the 2nd property of Side1Flash.

The exchanger duty is calculated by subtracting the side 1 outlet energy flow from the inlet.

Finally the log mean temperature difference is calculated in expression lmtd.

Objects.name: Overview
Objects.Notes:
Natural Gas Dew Point Control

Below is a diagram of the front end of a simple hydrocarbon dew point control process for natural gas. Externally created flowsheet SVG pasted into note The vapour from a feed stream is passed through a gas to gas exchanger and then a chiller, reducing the temperature to condense out heavier components. The vapour from the low temperature separator is then reheated in the gas to gas exchanger to become the sales gas, while pre-cooling the inlet separator vapour. The dew point of the sales gas is checked against a target value and the temperature of the low temperature separator is adjusted until that target is met. The feed conditions are known and given pressure drops for the gas to gas exchanger and chiller all that is needed is an initial estimate for the low temperature separator temperature to define it. A temperature approach between the inlet separator vapour and the sales gas allows the sale gas to be completely determined. With three of the four gas/gas stream known, a heat balance allows the temperature to the chiller to be determined. A refrigeration model from the ToolBox model is used for the chiller cooling. The liquids from the inlet and low temperature separators are fed to a stabilizer. A solver adjusts the overhead flow rate to meet a desired vapour pressure in the bottoms product. A phase envelopes for the feed and sales gas streams are plotted.

Objects.name: Overview1
Objects.Notes:
Simple Single Stage Refrigeration

This model shows how the properties of a simple single stage refrigeration loop can be calculated using basic thermodynamics. The refrigeration loop looks like this: The fluid being cooled has heat removed in the cooler by boiling the refrigerant. The resulting vapour is compressed to a higher pressure and hence a higher temperature. It is then condensed by an available coolant, here assumed to be air. The condensed high pressure liquid is then let down to a lower pressure through a valve. The lower pressure causes some of the liquid to vapourize and the phase rule dictates that for a given pressure a two phase fluid's temperature is determined from its phase envelope. Jumping ahead a bit, the graph below shows the phase envelope for the refrigerant we will use. It is just a line since we will use a pure component. The triangle represents the refrigerant conditions as it moves around the loop. The cooler conditions are at the lower left. Compressing the vapour raise both the temperature and pressure to the upper right point, while condensing moves it horizontally to the valve inlet condition at the upper left. Passing through the valve drops both temperature and pressure back to the cooler conditions.

Objects.name: Overview2
Objects.Notes: What we need to determine is: the pressures required for a required coolant temperature and available condensing temperature the flow rate of the refrigerant the duty of the condenser the power required for the compressor We will start with the refrigerant side of the cooler, represented by the flash tool called coolerOut. In this case we will assume a single component refrigerant difluormethane, commonly called R32 and so we will define the thermo parameter as: 'R32;massf,hflow which is simply as string with the component name(s). Here we have followed it with a double colon and the name(s) of the properties we want included in addition to the default ones. In this case, just the mass flow and energy flow. The mole fractions input can simply be set to 1 as there is only one component. We know the required coolant temperature and will set the first property to that. We also know that the coolant will be boiling, so we can set the second property to 1, which because it has a "Fraction" conversion unit type, will be taken as q, the vapour fraction. This means the vapour leaving the cooler should be a its dew point. This allows the pressure and other properties to be calculated, but the flow rate is still unknown. We will come back to that. Similar to the cooler, we know the condenser outlet temperature (presumably from available cooling) and can thus set the first property of the condenserOut flash tool. Since it is condensed, we can assume it will be at the bubble point and designate the second property to be 0. This will determine the condensing pressure and other properties. Since a valve has no heat inputs or outputs, it is isenthalpic, so we know the enthalpy of the fluid leaving the value and going to the cooler is the same as the liquid leaving the condenser. Back at the coolerOut Flash, we know the cooling load from InletQ and now that we know the enthalpy of the entering fluid, namely that of valveOut which is the same as that of condenserOut, the flow can be calculated by dividing the duty by the enthalpy difference in and out. With the flow rate known, we can calculate the condenser duty by the subtracting the energy flows of the inlet from the outlet, yielding a negative value. All that remains is to determine the required compressor power. For that we can copy and paste a previously made model representing a compressor from the toolbox and fill in the input expressions. That's it. All the values we wanted are now calculated. Note that the refrigerant can be changed in the thermo designation (R whatever, Propane, Ammonia, etc). If multiple components are used, the mole fraction spec will have to change accordingly.

Objects.name: Overview
Objects.Notes:
Polytropic Efficiency

This model calculates the polytropic efficiency for a compressor. The input expressions are: InletV - the molar volume of the inlet fluid inletP - the pressure of the inlet fluid inletH - the molar enthalpy of the inlet fluid Ideal - the flash results for the outlet fluid assuming isentropic compression. Outlet - the flash results for the actual outlet fluid The outlet expression is polyEff, the polytropic efficiency. The other expressions implement the calculation outlined below and where the expression calculates a variable mentioned here the the variable's symbol is listed in the expression notes.

Calculation overview

Polytropic efficiency can be defined as: Ep = Wp / Wa where: Ep = polytropic efficiency Wp = polytropic work Wa = actual work where the actual work Wa is: Wa = Ws / Ea where: Ea = adiabatic efficiency Ws = isentropic work and the adiabatic efficiency Eq can be calculated from: Ea = (hIout - hin) / (hAout - hin) where: hin is the enthalpy of the inlet fluid. hIOut is the enthalpy of the outlet for the ideal (isentropic) process. hAout is the enthalpy of the outlet for tne nonideal process. Back substituting Wa into the polytropic efficiency formula becomes: Ep = Ea * Wp / Ws The formulas for Wp and Ws are of the same form and after eliminating common terms from the numerator and denominator, we get Ep = Ea * ( n/(n-1) * ((p2/p1)^((n-1)/n) - 1) / ns/(ns-1) * ((p2/p1)^((ns-1)/ns) - 1) ) where: n = ln(p2/p1) / ln(v1/vs) ns = ln(p2/p1) / ln(v1/va) p1 = inlet pressure, p2 = outlet pressure v1 = inlet molar volume vs = isentropic outlet molar volume va = actual outlet molar volume

Objects.name: Overview
Objects.Notes:
Compressor

This model represents a thermodynamic model of a compressor, although it can also stand in for a pump. The input expressions are: feed - a flash result or similar representing the inlet fluid outletP - the outlet pressure to compress to. efficiency - the ideal power needed divided by the actual power needed The outlet expressions are: out - the outlet fluid flash power - the power required for the compression polyEff - the calculated polytropic efficiency An ideal compressor is first modeled by performing an isentropic flash using the outlet pressure and the feed entropy in tool IdealOut. The efficiency, e, of an non-ideal compressor is taken to be: e = (hIout - hin) / (hAout - hin) where: hin is the enthalpy of the inlet fluid hIOut is the enthalpy of the outlet for the ideal (isentropic) process hAout is the enthalpy of the outlet for tne nonideal process The desired efficiency is supplied in the input expression Efficiency so by rearranging, the expression H can calculate the nonideal outlet enthalpy, which is used with the outlet pressure to perform an isenthalpic flash in OutFluid. The power required for the compressor can then be calculated in expression Power by multiplying the flow by the difference between the outlet fluid enthalpy and the inlet fluid enthalpy.
